chapter_theme: Leaving Kanakamalai's city, Civakan hears his brother's counsel against trust and poison, crosses rich mountains to the hermitage, and is reunited with his mother Vijayai, now an ascetic.

cast.role: the hero, on his way from Kanakamalai's city to his mother
Civakan's younger brother (தம்பி), who counsels him and gives orders for his safety
Civakan's friend, charged with guarding him and sent to his mother
Saccandan's queen and Civakan's mother, now living as an ascetic in the hermitage (தேவி, அடிகள்)
those who say a tree has no life, mocked in 1907

1889.reading: As Civakan, his spear dripping blood and his garland woven of fragrant flowers and tender leaves, rides off on the maned horse, his younger brother speaks to him so that Padumukan among the gold-anklet warriors may hear.
1889.event: Civakan rides out from Kanakamalai's city and his younger brother begins to speak to him in Padumukan's hearing.
1889.nuance: The bowman (சிலையினான்) is Civakan and the speaker is his தம்பி, Nandattan, who came to him in the last ilampakam; the advice of the next verses is meant for Padumukan, who will carry it out.

1890.reading: The brother blesses Civakan: this world lies like a fine gem sunk in grime, waiting to be washed and to shine again, and the lady of the lotus does not embrace those who slip, so long may his garland flourish.

claims.claim: fortune does not embrace those who fail in their conduct

1890.nuance: The gem in grime is most likely the kingdom under the usurper, which Civakan must wash clean; lines 1 and 2 are hard to construe, and line 4 has a stray letter (புல்லாள்ட்).

1891.reading: He warns that weapons lie hidden in hands joined in worship, in a crown of hair, in weeping tears and in jewelled vessels, and kill when a fault is found, so trust no one's eyes: those who trusted have died.

claims.claim: no outward sign, not even reverence or tears, should be trusted, for those who trusted have perished

1891.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 take up the wording of Kural 828 (தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் ... அழுதகண் ணீரும்) with words inserted between (தொழுத தம் கையினுள்ளும், அழுத கண்ணீரினுள்ளும்), so it is not marked as an echo under the four-word rule, but the debt is plain. The epic extends the couplet's list to hair and jewel caskets, and closes on a judgment the couplet leaves unsaid: those who trusted are dead.

1892.reading: He orders that any women who are to touch the prince first be stripped of their ornaments, bathed in pure water and rubbed down by old women, then given white silk, garlands, sandal and fresh good ornaments, and only then let them embrace him.
1892.nuance: The danger is poison carried on a woman's body or jewels; line 2 (அரிறபத் திமிரி) reads corruptly.

1893.reading: Garlands, sandal, ornaments and clothes are not to be taken until their purity has been seen with the eyes, and the water and food he takes are to be guarded and tested with birds, the noble swan and the cock with its many hens.

claims.claim: nothing offered should be accepted until its purity has been examined

1893.nuance: Line 3 and the close of line 4 (யூகமோ டாய்க) are hard to fix: the birds seem to be poison-testers, and யூகம் may be judgment or a name.

1894.reading: As a snake no thicker than a collyrium stick, on a hill of waterfalls, kills an elephant with its sharp fang so that it falls bellowing, so no enemy should be called small, even one softer than cotton; one must guard against deceit as against the loss of a precious thing.

claims.claim: no enemy is small enough to be ignored; deceit must be guarded against

1895.reading: He bids them guard the one in their charge like a lizard in clinging close, like mothers in care, like great ascetics, like a tortoise in drawing in, like spear-bearing foes in cutting away harm, and like a wife in giving him delight.
1895.nuance: மதலை may mean the child (here Civakan, cherished like a son) or the prop of the house; the sense of the ascetics' simile (மருந்தவர்) is not certain.

1896.reading: Clothes, garlands, sandal, ornaments, the five scents and the measured prepared water, all these Padumukan, a lion among men, is to guard; so the broad-chested one commanded, and Padumukan did as told.
1896.event: Nandattan puts Padumukan in charge of everything that touches Civakan, and Padumukan carries out the order.
1896.nuance: The one who commands (ஏந்துபூண் மார்பன்) is taken to be the brother who has been speaking since 1889, but the epithet could fit Civakan.

1897.reading: On the way, a herd of small-eyed elephants tires, monkeys leap about not knowing a rock from what they take, and a yak, struck by fragrant sandal pieces, shrinks and spreads its hair.
1897.nuance: The mountain description opens; the order of who throws what at whom is hard to fix from the joined words.

1898.reading: On the famed hilltop, many-haired rats bigger than cats and red as coral dig up vermilion and pour it on the collyrium-dark hill, like the face-cloth on the brow of an elephant.

1899.reading: Where mountain goats leap on the peak, bright gems break and fall as dust, and every broad tree beneath looks like a wishing tree of heaven.
1899.nuance: Line 3 (விண்ணுளு வுண்டென) is doubtful; it may compare the falling dust to something in the sky.

1900.reading: Trees ripen near the deer, pythons lie sleeping in the forest like fallen palms, and when they wake the lion in its gold cave roars.
1900.nuance: Line 1 (கிலுத்தமற் றவற்றியற்) is hard to divide and probably corrupt.

1901.reading: On the slope, among timisu and sandal, the sweet-scented trees, takkolam, clove, camphor and musk spread their fragrance for a yojana.

1902.reading: Herds of large-eyed beasts stare at the young men, elephants in musth graze the sandal, deer scatter through the leafy woods and lions with lashing tails are everywhere.

1903.reading: Monkeys leap from jackfruit to jackfruit, gold flows down the hills like a rainbow fallen to earth, and the glow of gems climbs and splits the sky.

1904.reading: On that hard mountain slope the snow-rocks melt in the hot sun and flow like butter and honey, and the sandal wind through cloud-wrapped groves brings deep sorrow.
1904.nuance: The sorrow the sandal breeze brings is the separated lover's, a stock pain set into a landscape the hero crosses to reach his mother.

1905.reading: Through owls, costus and saffron spread over the hard land, the party lodges, rises and goes on, and comes with delight to a fine grove of naga trees where peacocks and swans cry together.
1905.event: Civakan's party crosses the hills and halts in a grove of naga trees.

1906.reading: There they spread cloth and covering, set out sandal, a gold thread-hung moonstone that drips water, saffron and diamond-set gold vessels, coral sugar, sandal fans, and in the place of the renouncers made a world of shining gems.
1906.event: The companions furnish a camp near the ascetics' grove.
1906.nuance: நீத்தவர் இடத்து, 'in the place of those who have renounced', sets the luxury beside the hermitage where Civakan's mother lives as an ascetic.

1907.reading: The narrator asks: see how the trees ripen and flower when the pearl-breasted women look at them with long eyes and touch them, and bow down to be plucked; can those who say a tree has no life be anything but madmen or ghouls?

claims.claim: trees are living beings, as their flowering at a woman's look and touch shows

1907.nuance: The flowering of trees at a woman's glance or touch is a poetic convention; here it is turned into an argument that plants live, a teaching Jains hold, though the verse names no school. The claim it mocks is answered in the same verse, so it is refuted here.

1908.reading: Civakan, more splendid than Murugan of the peacock, dismounts from his horse, lays aside the jewelled whip, sends his men away to go plainly and unseen, and says: tell the lady of the temple where peacocks call that it is time to receive me.
1908.event: Civakan dismounts, dismisses his retinue and sends to ask an audience of the ascetic lady at the shrine.
1908.nuance: He calls his mother அடிகள், the title of an ascetic: the queen he comes to meet is now a renouncer, and he puts off the signs of rank to approach her.

1909.reading: The queen says to a woman beside her that she saw a dream in the dark night, her eye throbs on the good side and a lizard has sounded there too: will her son come? Padumukan bows, falls at her good feet and says: lady, the prince has come.
1909.event: Vijayai reads a dream, a throbbing eye and a lizard's call as signs of her son's coming, and Padumukan announces that he has come.
1909.nuance: டேவி is தேவி after சொல்லினள் by sandhi; the queen is still called தேவி though she wears the ascetic's robe. Padumukan speaks the last line. In 1909 line 3 சோந்து looks corrupt.

1910.reading: When she asks where her lord's son is, he says 'I am your servant, lady', joins his bright bangled hands, worships and falls clasping her feet, and the two are like two seas of love mingling.
1910.event: Civakan falls at his mother Vijayai's feet and they embrace for the first time since his birth.
1910.nuance: Vijayai asks the question (ஐயன், the lord, here her son), and Civakan answers it himself with அடியன், 'your servant', the word of a worshipper to an ascetic as well as a son to a mother.

links.note: In 201 Saccandan hands his kingdom to Kattiyankaran out of trust; here the son's brother warns that those who trusted have died.
links.teaches: The brother's rule against trusting anyone is drawn from the family's own ruin, so the epic makes prudence an inheritance learned from the father's fatal trust.

links.note: The verse takes up the couplet's hands joined in worship and weeping tears that hide a weapon, adds hair and jewel caskets, and ends with those who trusted being dead.
links.teaches: The couplet names where a weapon hides; the epic turns it into a bodyguard's order and adds the outcome, showing the rule read as a practical protocol against poisoning.

gains.a: the brother's warning gains a known authority, so it reads as received wisdom rather than a young man's fear
gains.b: the couplet gains a situation and a consequence, a prince among strangers and the death of those who trusted

links.note: The couplet says to cut a thorn tree while young; the verse says no enemy, however soft and small, should be called small, using the snake that kills an elephant.
links.teaches: The couplet's remedy is to strike early, while the epic's is to guard always, so the same fear of a small foe yields attack in one and vigilance in the other.

gains.a: the verse's warning gains the couplet's point that a small foe grows, which explains why softness is no safety
gains.b: the couplet gains an alternative to striking first, the defence of a man who cannot yet fight his enemy openly

links.note: The couplet puts the lotus goddess in the effort of the unslothful; the verse says she will not embrace those who slip.
links.teaches: Where the Kural earns fortune by effort, the epic loses it by a lapse, so prosperity is shown as something kept by conduct and not only won by work.

gains.a: the blessing gains the couplet's account of what Lakshmi rewards, so the warning becomes a condition
gains.b: the couplet gains its negative side: fortune can be lost by one slip as well as missed by sloth

links.note: Neelakesi argues in debate that trees live, as their change with the seasons shows; the Cintamani's narrator says the same from their flowering at a woman's glance.
links.teaches: The Jain thesis that plants live appears both as a debater's proof and as a narrator's aside in a love scene, showing the doctrine was common enough to be argued from a poetic convention.

links.note: In Neelakesi 370 the Buddhist Mokkalan likens those who give trees life to men in madness; the Cintamani calls those who deny it madmen or ghouls.
links.teaches: The same charge of madness is thrown from both sides of the dispute over plant life, so the insult marks a live sectarian quarrel and not a settled view.

links.note: In 359 Vijayai, failing in spirit, watches the road for news of her son; here her watching ends when Padumukan announces him.
links.teaches: The long wait set up at the hermitage is closed by omens and then a messenger, so the mother's watch that began at his birth is fulfilled by the son's own coming rather than news of him.

links.note: In Akananuru 289 a wife waiting for her husband prays at each chirp of the lizard; here Vijayai reads the lizard's call, a dream and a throbbing eye as signs of her son.
links.teaches: The lizard omen of the akam wife waiting for her lover is given to a widowed mother in an ascetic's robe, showing that the epic carries the akam signs of reunion over to a son.

gains.a: Vijayai's omens gain their conventional sense from the akam waiting, which makes her longing read as near-erotic in intensity
gains.b: the akam image gains a non-erotic use, showing the omen signals any longed-for return, not only a lover's

links.note: In 318 Vijayai suckles the newborn, puts her husband's ring on him and leaves him; here the grown son falls at her feet.
links.teaches: The parting at birth and the reunion are linked by the son's self-naming as her servant, so the child she gave up returns as a worshipper of the renouncer she has become.

new_concepts.gloss: a blessing or wish spoken for another's welfare
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's blessing வாழ்க நுங் கண்ணி (1890, line 4); id as declared in earlier Cintamani chapters

source_issues: Most verses of 1889-1910 (except 1896-1905, 1909) were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); word division inside joined lines is often doubtful.
1890 line 4 has a stray letter: புல்லாள்ட்.
1900 line 1 கிலுத்தமற் றவற்றியற் divides doubtfully and may be corrupt.
